problem.q: Is this really a problem today?
problem.a: Yes! It’s a massive problem, but most Christians are completely unaware of it because they have a Bible or have access to one they can read online. Because it is so easy to read a Bible online, the assumption is that the Bible must be easy to use and share, right? But anyone who has tried to get access to Scripture to **make** something (an app, a website, a new Bible translation, an audio Bible, etc.) knows that is not the case. And for a world that desperately needs the gospel, this is completely inexcusable.

attribution.q: What’s wrong with requiring others to attribute the creator of a Bible translation?
attribution.a: Requesting attribution is fine. **Requiring it** adds a human condition to passing on God’s word. Anyone may still copy, translate, revise, adapt, and distribute it, so we count it as viable, but it falls short of giving freely.

shareAlike.q: Isn’t share-alike a good way to protect Scripture?
shareAlike.a: Share-alike was built as a response to copyright in order to prevent anyone taking an open text, changing it, and locking the result away. It keeps all five uses (copying, translating, revising, adapting, and distributing) open, so we count it as viable. But it still forbids faithful work: a translator who builds on a share-alike text cannot release their translation into the public domain. But we would advocate that copyright is not the best response to copyright. Rather, the higher goal should be **so much** quality, public-domain material that anyone can adapt whatever they need for the kingdom.

conditions.q: What if I still want to put conditions on my translation?
conditions.a: Then at least make exceptions easy. Publish how to reach you, answer quickly, and grant exceptions for faithful uses. Plan who will answer when you no longer can, or release your work into the public domain at your death. If you cannot keep that up, release it now. Every request left unanswered closes a door for the kingdom, and even a quick yes fails the believer who cannot safely ask from a persecuted context.

money.q: But how will Bible translators and publishers make money?

nonCommercial.q: What’s wrong with requiring noncommercial use?
nonCommercial.a: Non-commercial terms forbid faithful work, so we count them as restricted. There are many ways a Bible could be distributed commercially in a pure and faithful manner (for example, printing Bibles and selling them at just the price required to make a small profit to reinvest in the operation and increase distribution). The point, dear Christian, is that it is simply **not your place** to tell others how they can and cannot use God’s word.

fund.title: Free Use Fund
fund.sub: We’re launching a project-based fund to kickstart an open ecosystem for global Christianity.
fund.whatBody1: Our vision is a growing ecosystem of Christians creating high-quality public-domain resources and open-source tools from one another’s work.
fund.whatBody2: We fund technology, tools, and shared resources that grow the global Christian ecosystem: Bible translations and audio, datasets, maps, charts, assets, software, and platforms. We prioritize projects with the widest potential impact and especially encourage individuals and small teams, since funding will be limited as the fund grows. We favor CC0 content and open-source software under licenses such as MIT or AGPL. Each release gives the next builder more to work with.
fund.overview: Read the Free Use Fund overview
fund.statusBody: This is the fund’s first cycle, and AO Lab’s annual support goal of {{ goal }} has not yet been met, so the Free Use Fund currently has no money. You can view the current support status {{ here }}.
fund.callIntro: New projects and work already underway are both welcome. Tell us:

build.title: What you intend to build.
build.body: Describe the project, who would be involved, and what support you might need.

licences.title: The proposed licenses.
licences.body: State the licenses for the content, software, and any existing material you would use.

why.title: Why it matters.
why.body: Explain its value to the open ecosystem we are building for global Christianity.

fund.reportingBody: We will publish quarterly progress updates covering which projects were funded and the status of ongoing and completed work.

who.a: Anyone in the general public, including individuals, teams, churches, ministries, and organizations. Describe what you want to build, its proposed licenses, and why it matters to the open ecosystem serving global Christianity.

early.q: Why submit before funding is available?
early.a: Your proposals help us identify needs and show what support could make possible. They can help us raise support for AO Lab and the wider community, and give us projects to consider when funding becomes available.

decides.q: Who decides which projects receive funding?
decides.a: AO Lab manages the fund and selects projects by their expected kingdom impact and benefit to the wider Church. Projects may be large or small, with priority given to work that the largest community can use and build upon. Because the fund aims for maximum global impact, we lean toward web-based solutions that anyone can reach, though this is not a requirement.

staff.a: Yes. Anyone is welcome to apply, including AO Lab staff, and we fund the projects we believe will best advance the kingdom. The fund is designed to grow the wider ecosystem beyond our own team, so our heavy bias is to fund outward. We expect staff funding to be minor, but we won’t rule it out when someone on our team is clearly the best person for a high-impact project.

commission.q: Does AO Lab commission projects or run events?
commission.a: Yes. Alongside open proposals, we may identify critical gaps in the ecosystem and invite capable individuals or teams to take them on. As the fund grows, we may also put perhaps 5% to 10% toward hackathons, prizes, and collaborative sprints that bring new builders into the work and produce freely reusable resources. That is a guideline, not a quota: when worthy projects need funding, the money goes to the projects.

money.q: How does money reach the fund?
money.a: From September onward, we raise AO Lab’s annual operating support for the coming year ({{ goal }} for this cycle). Once that goal is met, 100% of additional gifts go to the Free Use Fund until the next September cycle begins. Because this is our first cycle, we may adjust the annual goal or shift timelines as we see the fruit of this approach.

licences.a: We prefer the most permissive terms possible, with CC0 as the standard for content such as translations, datasets, and assets. We are open to other licenses for content, but only when a strong case is made. Software may use MIT, AGPL, or other open-source licenses. We review software licensing case by case, considering how well it supports reuse and the wider ecosystem. State your proposed licenses in your proposal.

translation.q: Could the fund support a Bible translation?
translation.a: Yes, though our preference is to fund capabilities, tools, and datasets that help translators create higher-quality resources more quickly. A CC0 Bible translation can be considered alongside other resources and open-source tools, but we prefer work that serves the greatest need. We evaluate projects by their potential kingdom impact and shared benefit, rather than giving one type of work automatic priority.

progress.q: Where can I follow spending and project progress?
progress.a: On this page. Quarterly updates will show how money was spent and which projects it supported, including unfinished work. Completed projects will be published and announced as they are finished.

public.q: Will every project’s details be public?
public.a: Not always. We may withhold information that could endanger people working in persecuted regions. Builders may also choose to stay anonymous in anything we publish, as long as they share their name and email with us so we can verify them and their work. Quarterly reporting will continue either way, with those details withheld. Funders are welcome to {{ contact }} to discuss what can safely be shared.
